title: FCFS & Shortest Job First
summary: The two simplest schedulers, worked with real numbers, the convoy effect, and why SJF is provably optimal yet impractical to use exactly as described.

slides.markdown:
**First-Come-First-Served (FCFS)** runs jobs in arrival order, no exceptions — dead simple, but a short job can get stuck behind a long one. **Shortest Job First (SJF)** always runs whichever ready job has the smallest remaining burst — provably the best possible average waiting time, but it needs to know burst times in advance, which real systems don't.

This topic works both with real numbers on a Gantt chart, so you can compute waiting and turnaround times cold in an interview, not just describe the algorithms in words.

FCFS is exactly what it sounds like: processes are served strictly in arrival order, and once a process starts running it keeps the CPU until it finishes (FCFS is non-preemptive) — no other process can interrupt it, no matter how long it takes.

Implementation-wise it's a plain FIFO queue: enqueue on arrival, dequeue and run to completion, repeat. There's no decision-making complexity at all, which is exactly its appeal for the simplest possible systems, and exactly its weakness for anything with mixed job lengths.

The next slide computes it with real numbers so the trade-off becomes concrete rather than theoretical.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: FCFS Gantt chart and average wait time
slides.markdown:
Three processes, all arriving at time 0 (arrival order = the order listed): P1 burst 24, P2 burst 3, P3 burst 3.

```
Gantt chart:
| P1 (0-24) | P2 (24-27) | P3 (27-30) |
0          24           27          30

Waiting time = start time - arrival time (all arrive at 0):
P1: 0
P2: 24
P3: 27

Average waiting time = (0 + 24 + 27) / 3 = 17
```

P1's 24-unit burst forces P2 and P3 — each only 3 units of actual work — to wait an enormous 24 and 27 units respectively. The average of 17 is dragged up entirely by an ordering accident, not by any process actually needing that much CPU: this exact scenario is what the next two slides name and fix.

slides.sectionTitle: The convoy effect — short jobs stuck behind long ones
slides.markdown:
The **convoy effect** is exactly the pattern the worked example just showed: a handful of short, cheap processes queue up behind one long process, like a line of fast cars stuck behind a slow truck on a single-lane road with no way to pass.

It's especially damaging when the long process is CPU-bound and the short ones are I/O-bound: the I/O-bound processes would normally issue a quick request and yield, but under strict FCFS they can't even get a turn to issue that request until the long job finishes — starving I/O devices of work and hurting overall system utilization, not just those processes' individual wait times.

The root cause is structural, not bad luck: FCFS makes no distinction between a 1-unit job and a 1000-unit job, so ordering alone determines outcomes, and a single badly-timed long arrival degrades everything behind it.

slides.sectionTitle: Shortest Job First: minimizing average waiting time
slides.markdown:
SJF flips FCFS's rule: instead of arrival order, always run whichever ready process has the smallest burst time. Using the exact same three processes from the FCFS example (P1=24, P2=3, P3=3, all arriving at 0), SJF would run P2 and P3 first, then P1: order P2, P3, P1 (tie broken arbitrarily since P2 and P3 are equal).

```
Gantt chart:
| P2 (0-3) | P3 (3-6) | P1 (6-30) |
0         3          6            30

Waiting time:
P2: 0
P3: 3
P1: 6

Average waiting time = (0 + 3 + 6) / 3 = 3
```

Same three processes, same total work — average waiting time dropped from 17 (FCFS) to 3, purely from reordering. This isn't a lucky example; it's the general pattern SJF exploits every time job lengths vary.

slides.sectionTitle: Why SJF is provably optimal for average wait time
slides.markdown:
SJF isn't just empirically good in this example — it's mathematically provable that no scheduling order can beat it on average waiting time, for a fixed, known set of burst times. The intuition: every unit of time a short job waits behind a longer one adds that job's wait, while running the short job first only delays the long job by that short amount — moving a shorter job earlier always removes more total waiting than it adds.

This is a classic exchange-argument proof: take any non-SJF schedule, find two adjacent jobs out of shortest-first order, swap them, and total waiting time never increases (and strictly decreases if they were genuinely out of order) — repeating this until no swaps are possible arrives at the SJF order.

The catch that keeps SJF from being used as-is: this optimality assumes you already *know* each job's exact burst time before running it, which is the subject of the very next slide.

slides.sectionTitle: The catch: SJF needs to predict burst time
slides.markdown:
A real scheduler doesn't know how long a process will run before it starts — burst time isn't a property the OS is told in advance, it's an outcome of what the program does. SJF's optimality is only reachable if this unknown is somehow estimated.

The standard technique is **exponential averaging**: predict the next burst as a weighted combination of the actual previous burst and the previous prediction, `next = α × actual_previous + (1 − α) × previous_prediction`, where `α` (commonly 0.5) controls how much weight recent behavior gets versus history. A process with a history of short bursts gets predicted short; one with a history of long bursts gets predicted long — reasonably accurate for processes with consistent behavior, poor for erratic ones.

This is why real OSes don't implement literal SJF — they implement approximations of its spirit (Linux's CFS and MLFQ-style feedback queues, both covered later in this group) using *observed* recent behavior as a proxy for future burst length, rather than a promised, known value.

slides.sectionTitle: Preemptive SJF = Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF)
slides.markdown:
Plain SJF is non-preemptive: once a job starts, even a newly-arrived shorter job has to wait for it to finish. **Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF)** is SJF's preemptive version: whenever a new process arrives, compare its burst time to the *remaining* time of whatever's currently running, and preempt immediately if the new arrival is shorter.

This matters a lot when jobs arrive at different times rather than all at once — a long job that started first can still be interrupted the moment a much shorter job shows up, rather than forcing that short job to wait out the long one's entire remaining burst.

SRTF retains SJF's optimality (still provably minimal average waiting time, now for the dynamic-arrival case) at the cost of more context switches — every preemption decision has real dispatch-latency overhead, same trade-off as any preemptive scheme.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: SRTF Gantt chart with a shorter job arriving mid-execution
slides.markdown:
P1 arrives at 0 with burst 8. P2 arrives at 1 with burst 4. Under SRTF: P1 starts at 0 (nothing else is ready). At time 1, P2 arrives with remaining-time 4 versus P1's remaining 7 — P2 is shorter, so P1 is preempted.

```
Gantt chart:
| P1 (0-1) | P2 (1-5) | P1 resumes (5-12) |
0         1          5                   12

P1: arrival 0, first ran 0-1, preempted, resumed 5-12, completion 12
    turnaround = 12 - 0 = 12,  waiting = 12 - 8 (burst) = 4
P2: arrival 1, ran 1-5 uninterrupted, completion 5
    turnaround = 5 - 1 = 4,   waiting = 4 - 4 (burst) = 0

Average waiting time = (4 + 0) / 2 = 2
```

Under plain non-preemptive SJF, P2 would have had to wait the full 7 remaining units of P1 before even starting — SRTF's preemption is what drops P2's wait to 0 while only adding 4 units of total wait to P1.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: starvation of long jobs under SJF/SRTF
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "SJF is provably optimal, so it's simply the best scheduler to use."

**Why it's wrong:** optimality here is specifically about *average* waiting time across a fixed batch — it says nothing about worst-case fairness. If short jobs keep arriving in a steady stream, a long job can be preempted (under SRTF) or passed over (under SJF) indefinitely, since there's always something shorter ready to run first — this is textbook **starvation**, and it can genuinely never resolve under a naive implementation with continuous arrivals.

**Correct model:** any deployment of SJF/SRTF needs an explicit anti-starvation mechanism layered on top — **aging**, where a waiting job's effective priority (or apparent burst time) improves the longer it waits, eventually guaranteeing it runs regardless of what keeps arriving. Optimal-on-average and fair-in-the-worst-case are different properties, and SJF alone only gives you the first.

slides.sectionTitle: Senior nuance: why real OSes never implement literal SJF
slides.markdown:
Beyond the prediction problem, literal SJF has a second issue that makes it unsuitable for a general-purpose scheduler as-is: it requires comparing burst times across *all* ready processes on every scheduling decision, and it optimizes purely for throughput/waiting time with no notion of user-perceived priority, interactivity, or fairness guarantees a real OS needs to provide (a background compile job could still legitimately delay a foreground click if it happened to look "shorter" by the predictor's estimate).

Production schedulers borrow SJF's *core insight* — favor processes that behave like they'll finish or yield soon — without adopting it wholesale. Linux's MLFQ-style legacy scheduler inferred "probably short and interactive" from a process's history of quickly yielding the CPU (I/O-bound behavior), and CFS's vruntime-based fairness produces SJF-like behavior for I/O-bound tasks as a side effect of fairness, not as an explicit burst-time prediction.

The interview-ready framing: SJF is the *ideal* every practical scheduler approximates, not an algorithm anyone actually ships unmodified.

slides.sectionTitle: How this shows up in production
slides.markdown:
The convoy effect shows up constantly outside CPU scheduling. A single-threaded database connection processing queries strictly in submission order will let one slow analytical query block many fast lookups behind it — the exact same convoy pattern, one layer up in an application queue instead of a kernel scheduler.

Message queue systems (RabbitMQ, SQS) that support **priority queues** or separate fast/slow lanes are directly borrowing SJF's insight: route short, cheap jobs to a lane that isn't blocked behind long-running ones, rather than processing everything in one strict FCFS order.

When debugging "why is this specific fast request taking forever even though the server isn't overloaded," checking whether it's queued behind a slow one in a single FCFS-style lane is often the fastest diagnosis — the exact failure mode this topic names and quantifies.
